history.q: In what year was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
history.fact: The Second Continental Congress adopted it in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776; Thomas Jefferson was its principal author.

history.q: Who was the first President of the United States?
history.fact: Washington took the oath in 1789 on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City, which was then the nation's capital.

history.q: Which ship carried the Pilgrims to Plymouth in 1620?
history.fact: Before landing, the passengers signed the Mayflower Compact, an early agreement to govern themselves by majority rule.

history.q: From which country did the United States purchase Alaska in 1867?
history.fact: Secretary of State William Seward paid $7.2 million, about 2 cents an acre; critics mocked the deal as "Seward's Folly."

history.q: From which country did the United States buy the Louisiana Territory in 1803?
history.fact: Napoleon sold the territory for about $15 million, roughly doubling the size of the young United States overnight.

history.q: What was the first permanent English settlement in North America, founded in 1607?
history.fact: Jamestown, Virginia, survived early famine and later served as the colony's capital until 1699.

history.q: In what year was the 19th Amendment, guaranteeing women the right to vote, ratified?
history.fact: Tennessee clinched ratification after 24-year-old legislator Harry Burn switched his vote, following a letter from his mother.

history.q: Which president sent Lewis and Clark on their 1804-1806 expedition to the Pacific?
history.fact: Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone woman, served as an interpreter for the expedition; she appears on a US dollar coin first issued in 2000.

history.q: Which British general surrendered at Yorktown in 1781, effectively ending major fighting in the Revolutionary War?
history.fact: French troops under Rochambeau and a French fleet under de Grasse were crucial to trapping the British army at Yorktown.

history.q: The first transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869 at Promontory Summit, in which present-day state?
history.fact: A ceremonial golden spike was driven on May 10, 1869, joining the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines.

history.q: Which president delivered the Gettysburg Address in November 1863?
history.fact: The speech ran fewer than 300 words and took about two minutes, yet it became one of the most quoted speeches in American history.

history.q: Where did Japan's surprise attack of December 7, 1941, which brought the US into World War II, take place?
history.fact: The attack on the Hawaii naval base damaged or sank all eight US battleships there; Roosevelt called it "a date which will live in infamy."

history.q: Which civil rights leader delivered the "I Have a Dream" speech in 1963?
history.fact: King spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, before a crowd of about 250,000.

history.q: In which 1773 protest did colonists dump chests of British tea into Boston Harbor?
history.fact: Protesters, some disguised as Mohawk warriors, emptied 342 chests of East India Company tea into the harbor.

history.q: Gold found at Sutter's Mill in 1848 sparked a famous rush to which present-day state?
history.fact: About 300,000 "forty-niners" poured in, and California went from territory to statehood in just 1850.

history.q: The American Civil War began in April 1861 with a Confederate attack on which fort?
history.fact: The fort sits in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina; remarkably, no soldiers were killed by enemy fire during the 34-hour bombardment.

history.q: Which Confederate general surrendered at Appomattox Court House in April 1865?
history.fact: Lee surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of Wilmer McLean's house; Grant let Lee's men keep their horses for spring planting.

history.q: Which president launched the New Deal in response to the Great Depression?
history.fact: Roosevelt's radio "fireside chats" explained his policies directly to millions of listeners gathered around their home sets.

history.q: Which 1954 Supreme Court decision ruled racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional?
history.fact: The decision was unanimous; the lead lawyer, Thurgood Marshall, later became the first Black justice on the Supreme Court.

history.q: Which writer's 1776 pamphlet "Common Sense" made a popular case for American independence?
history.fact: Published anonymously in January 1776, the pamphlet became a runaway bestseller and was read aloud in taverns across the colonies.

history.q: Which 1787 law set out how lands northwest of the Ohio River would become states, and banned slavery there?
history.fact: Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin, plus part of Minnesota, were eventually carved from the Northwest Territory.

history.q: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state alongside which new free state?
history.fact: Maine had been part of Massachusetts; the deal also barred slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of latitude 36°30′.

history.q: Which 1777 American victory, ending in a British army's surrender, helped persuade France to join the war?
history.fact: British General John Burgoyne surrendered his army at Saratoga; France signed a treaty of alliance with the Americans in 1778.

history.q: Which 1862 law offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on and farmed it for five years?
history.fact: Over the following decades, around 1.6 million homestead claims transferred some 10% of all US land into private hands.

history.q: Which treaty, signed in December 1814, ended the War of 1812?
history.fact: It was signed in present-day Belgium; news crossed the Atlantic so slowly that the Battle of New Orleans was fought weeks later.

technology.q: Which brothers made the first controlled, sustained powered airplane flights in 1903?
technology.fact: The first flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, lasted 12 seconds and covered 120 feet, shorter than a Boeing 747's wingspan.

technology.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon, in July 1969?
technology.fact: While Armstrong and Aldrin explored the surface, Michael Collins orbited alone in the Apollo 11 command module, Columbia.

technology.q: Who received the 1876 US patent for the telephone?
technology.fact: Bell was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, and worked as a teacher of the deaf before his telephone experiments in Boston.

technology.q: Which Ford car, introduced in 1908, put motoring within reach of ordinary Americans?
technology.fact: Ford's moving assembly line, introduced in 1913, cut the time to build a Model T from about 12 hours to roughly 90 minutes.

technology.q: Thomas Edison's famous research laboratory was located in which New Jersey town?
technology.fact: Nicknamed "The Wizard of Menlo Park," Edison invented the phonograph there in 1877.

technology.q: What was the code name of the World War II US project that developed the first atomic bombs?
technology.fact: Its main weapons laboratory, at Los Alamos, New Mexico, was directed by physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer.

technology.q: Which American scientist developed the first widely used polio vaccine, announced in 1955?
technology.fact: Asked who owned the patent, Salk famously replied, "There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?"

technology.q: Which company introduced the first commercial microprocessor, the 4004, in 1971?
technology.fact: The Intel 4004 packed about 2,300 transistors and was originally designed for a Japanese calculator maker, Busicom.

technology.q: What was the first satellite launched by the United States, in January 1958?
technology.fact: Explorer 1 carried an instrument by James Van Allen that discovered the radiation belts now named after him.

technology.q: ARPANET, a precursor of the internet, sent its first message in 1969 from which university?
technology.fact: The first message was meant to be "LOGIN," but the system crashed after just two letters, "LO."

technology.q: Which Founding Father is famous for a kite experiment showing that lightning is electricity?
technology.fact: Franklin also invented the lightning rod, bifocal glasses and the Franklin stove, and never patented any of them.

technology.q: Which company did Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak co-found in 1976?
technology.fact: Their first product, the Apple I, was sold as a bare circuit board for $666.66.

technology.q: Samuel Morse sent the message "What hath God wrought" in 1844 using which invention?
technology.fact: Before turning to invention, Morse was an accomplished portrait painter who studied art in London.

technology.q: Which company did Larry Page and Sergey Brin found in a Menlo Park garage in 1998?
technology.fact: The name plays on "googol," the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.

technology.q: Which president set the goal, in 1961, of landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out?
technology.fact: He set the goal before Congress in May 1961; his famous "We choose to go to the Moon" speech came at Rice University in 1962.

technology.q: Who invented the cotton gin in 1793?
technology.fact: Whitney later won a government contract to make muskets and became a champion of interchangeable parts.

technology.q: Cyrus McCormick is famous for which farm invention of the 1830s?
technology.fact: McCormick's Chicago factory, opened in 1847, helped make the city a hub of the farm machinery industry.

technology.q: Who became the first American woman in space, aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger in 1983?
technology.fact: At 32, Ride was also the youngest American to have flown in space at the time; she trained as a physicist at Stanford.

technology.q: Which company launched its influential Personal Computer, model 5150, in 1981?
technology.fact: The IBM PC ran PC DOS, an operating system licensed from a then-small company called Microsoft.

technology.q: Who became the first American to orbit the Earth, in 1962?
technology.fact: In 1998, at age 77, Glenn flew again aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery, becoming the oldest person in space at the time.

technology.q: What was the name of the first US space station, launched in 1973?
technology.fact: Skylab fell back to Earth in 1979, scattering debris across remote parts of Western Australia.

technology.q: ENIAC, an early general-purpose electronic computer unveiled in 1946, was built at which university?
technology.fact: ENIAC weighed about 27 tonnes and used nearly 18,000 vacuum tubes, filling a large room.

technology.q: Which co-inventor of the transistor at Bell Labs went on to win a second Nobel Prize in Physics?
technology.fact: Bardeen won in 1956 for the transistor and in 1972 for the theory of superconductivity, the only person to win the physics prize twice.

technology.q: Which chemist invented nylon while working at DuPont in the 1930s?
technology.fact: When nylon stockings went on sale nationwide in 1940, shoppers mobbed stores to buy them.

technology.q: Who drilled the 1859 well in Titusville, Pennsylvania, that launched the US oil industry?
technology.fact: Drake struck oil at a depth of about 69.5 feet (21 m), but he never patented his drilling method and died in modest circumstances.

art.q: Which American painter is famous for his "drip" paintings?
art.fact: Pollock often laid his canvases flat on the floor and poured or flung paint onto them, working from all sides.

art.q: Which artist created the 1962 work "Campbell's Soup Cans"?
art.fact: The work consists of 32 canvases, one for each variety of soup Campbell's sold at the time.

art.q: Who wrote "The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn"?
art.fact: "Mark Twain" was the pen name of Samuel Clemens, taken from a riverboat call meaning two fathoms (12 feet) of water: safe to pass.

art.q: Which musical genre emerged in New Orleans in the early 20th century?
art.fact: Louis Armstrong, born in New Orleans in 1901, became one of jazz's most influential trumpeters and singers.

art.q: Who painted "Nighthawks" (1942), showing late-night diners in a corner restaurant?
art.fact: The Art Institute of Chicago bought "Nighthawks" in 1942, the year it was painted, for $3,000.

art.q: Which architect designed Fallingwater, a house built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania?
art.fact: Designed in 1935 for the Kaufmann family, Fallingwater's concrete terraces cantilever over the Bear Run stream.

art.q: Which Harper Lee novel won the 1961 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction?
art.fact: The book's fictional town of Maycomb, Alabama, was modeled on Lee's hometown of Monroeville.

art.q: Which American composer wrote "Rhapsody in Blue" (1924)?
art.fact: The piece opens with a famous rising clarinet glissando; Gershwin himself played the piano at its 1924 New York premiere.

art.q: Georgia O'Keeffe is especially associated with the landscapes of which US state, where she lived later in life?
art.fact: The Georgia O'Keeffe Museum opened in Santa Fe, New Mexico, in 1997, holding the largest collection of her work.

art.q: Which 1927 film was the first feature-length movie with synchronized spoken dialogue?
art.fact: Star Al Jolson's ad-libbed line "You ain't heard nothin' yet!" became one of the first spoken lines in a feature film.

art.q: Which singer is known as the "King of Rock and Roll"?
art.fact: His Memphis mansion, Graceland, opened to the public in 1982 and is one of the most visited private homes in America.

art.q: Who wrote "The Great Gatsby" (1925)?
art.fact: The novel sold modestly in Fitzgerald's lifetime; it became a classic only after copies were given to US troops during World War II.

art.q: Which animator and studio founder created Mickey Mouse?
art.fact: Mickey's 1928 debut hit, "Steamboat Willie," was one of the first cartoons with fully synchronized sound.

art.q: Which Broadway musical by Lin-Manuel Miranda tells the story of a Founding Father through hip-hop?
art.fact: "Hamilton" won 11 Tony Awards in 2016 and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

art.q: Which writer wrote the poem "The Raven" (1845)?
art.fact: Poe is also credited with inventing the modern detective story with "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" (1841).

art.q: Which artist painted "American Gothic" (1930)?
art.fact: The models for the stern farm pair were Wood's sister Nan and his dentist; the painting hangs in the Art Institute of Chicago.

art.q: Which author wrote "The Grapes of Wrath" (1939) about Dust Bowl migrants?
art.fact: The novel won the 1940 Pulitzer Prize, and Steinbeck went on to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962.

art.q: Which poet wrote the collection "Leaves of Grass"?
art.fact: Whitman self-published the first edition in 1855 and kept revising and expanding it for the rest of his life.

art.q: Which choreographer created "Revelations" (1960), a dance set to African American spirituals?
art.fact: Performed by the company Ailey founded in 1958, "Revelations" is one of the most widely seen modern dance works in the world.

art.q: Beale Street, celebrated as the "Home of the Blues," is in which city?
art.fact: W. C. Handy, the "Father of the Blues," worked there and published "Beale Street Blues" in 1916.

art.q: Which composer wrote the ballet score "Appalachian Spring" (1944)?
art.fact: Written for Martha Graham's company, it quotes the Shaker hymn "Simple Gifts" and won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize for Music.

art.q: Which painter is considered the founder of the Hudson River School of landscape art?
art.fact: English-born Cole painted the Catskills and Hudson Valley, launching what is often called America's first native art movement.

art.q: Who wrote the 1952 novel "Invisible Man"?
art.fact: It won the 1953 National Book Award and was the only novel Ellison published in his lifetime.

art.q: Which architect designed the Gateway Arch in St. Louis?
art.fact: Completed in 1965, the stainless-steel arch stands 630 feet (192 m) tall, making it the world's tallest arch.

art.q: Which Toni Morrison novel won the 1988 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction?
art.fact: In 1993 Morrison became the first Black woman to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

politics.q: How many senators does each US state elect?
politics.fact: Since the 17th Amendment (1913), senators have been elected directly by voters rather than chosen by state legislatures.

politics.q: How long is a single US presidential term?
politics.fact: The 22nd Amendment (1951) limits presidents to two elected terms, a response to Franklin D. Roosevelt's four election victories.

politics.q: Which president issued the Emancipation Proclamation?
politics.fact: Issued on January 1, 1863, during the Civil War; the 13th Amendment abolished slavery nationwide in 1865.

politics.q: What are the first ten amendments to the US Constitution collectively called?
politics.fact: Ratified in 1791, the Bill of Rights was drafted largely by James Madison and protects freedoms such as speech and religion.

politics.q: How many justices sit on the US Supreme Court?
politics.fact: The number of justices is set by Congress, not the Constitution, and has stayed at nine since 1869.

politics.q: How many electoral votes does a candidate need to win the US presidency?
politics.fact: The Electoral College has 538 electors: one for each member of Congress plus three for Washington, D.C.

politics.q: Who is the only US president to have resigned from office?
politics.fact: Nixon resigned in August 1974; his successor Gerald Ford became the only president never elected as president or vice president.

politics.q: In which city was the US Constitution drafted in 1787?
politics.fact: The Constitutional Convention met in Independence Hall, the same building where the Declaration of Independence was adopted.

politics.q: Which 1803 Supreme Court case established the principle of judicial review?
politics.fact: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote that it is "emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is."

politics.q: Which document served as the first constitution of the United States, before the current Constitution took effect in 1789?
politics.fact: Ratified in 1781, the Articles created a weak central government that could not levy taxes, prompting calls for a new constitution.

politics.q: Which building in Washington, D.C., is the official residence of the US president?
politics.fact: John Adams was the first president to live there, moving in in November 1800 while the house was still unfinished.

politics.q: What is the minimum age to serve as US president?
politics.fact: The youngest to take office was Theodore Roosevelt at 42; John F. Kennedy was the youngest ever elected, at 43.

politics.q: Which animal is the symbol of the Republican Party?
politics.fact: Cartoonist Thomas Nast popularized both the Republican elephant and the Democratic donkey in the 1870s.

politics.q: In which month are US presidential elections held?
politics.fact: Election Day falls on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November, a date Congress set in 1845.

politics.q: Which branch of the US government does the Supreme Court head?
politics.fact: The Court had no building of its own until 1935; for decades it met in rooms inside the US Capitol.

politics.q: Who is known as the "Father of the Constitution"?
politics.fact: Madison's detailed notes are the best record of the 1787 Convention; he later became the fourth president.

politics.q: Which amendment to the US Constitution abolished slavery?
politics.fact: It was ratified in December 1865, eight months after Abraham Lincoln's assassination.

politics.q: Under the Constitution, who serves as President of the US Senate?
politics.fact: The vice president may cast a vote in the Senate only to break a tie.

politics.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1951, limits a president to two elected terms?
politics.fact: It also says that anyone who serves more than two years of another president's term can be elected only once.

politics.q: How many voting members sit in the US House of Representatives?
politics.fact: The House has been capped at 435 voting seats since 1913, apart from a brief rise to 437 after Alaska and Hawaii joined.

politics.q: Which 1966 Supreme Court case requires police to inform suspects of their rights before questioning?
politics.fact: The familiar warning, "You have the right to remain silent," is known as the Miranda warning after Ernesto Miranda.

politics.q: Who was the first Chief Justice of the United States?
politics.fact: While still Chief Justice, Jay negotiated the 1794 Jay Treaty with Britain; he also co-wrote the Federalist Papers.

politics.q: Which amendment, used for the first time in 1973, provides for filling a vacancy in the vice presidency?
politics.fact: Gerald Ford became vice president under it and then president, without ever being elected to either office.

politics.q: Which 1965 law signed by Lyndon B. Johnson outlawed discriminatory voting practices such as literacy tests?
politics.fact: Johnson signed it in August 1965, just months after the Selma-to-Montgomery marches.

politics.q: Before Donald Trump, who was the only US president to serve two non-consecutive terms?
politics.fact: Cleveland was both the 22nd and 24th president; he lost in 1888 to Benjamin Harrison, then beat him in 1892.

current-affairs.q: Who won the November 2020 US presidential election?
current-affairs.fact: Before becoming vice president under Barack Obama, Biden served 36 years as a US senator from Delaware.

current-affairs.q: Who became the first woman to serve as US Vice President, sworn in in January 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Harris was also the first Black American and the first South Asian American to hold the office.

current-affairs.q: Who won the November 2024 US presidential election?
current-affairs.fact: Trump became the second president to serve two non-consecutive terms, after Grover Cleveland (1885-89 and 1893-97).

current-affairs.q: Which NFL team won Super Bowl LVIII in February 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Played in Las Vegas, it was the city's first Super Bowl and only the second in history to go to overtime.

current-affairs.q: Which NASA rover landed in Mars's Jezero Crater in February 2021?
current-affairs.fact: It carried Ingenuity, a small helicopter that made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet in April 2021.

current-affairs.q: Which NASA-led space telescope, launched in December 2021, released its first full-color science images in July 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Webb observes from around the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth, shielded by a tennis-court-sized sunshade.

current-affairs.q: Who became the first Black woman to serve on the US Supreme Court, in June 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Jackson succeeded Justice Stephen Breyer, for whom she had once worked as a law clerk.

current-affairs.q: Which Baltimore bridge collapsed in March 2024 after being struck by a container ship?
current-affairs.fact: The bridge was named for Francis Scott Key, who wrote the words of "The Star-Spangled Banner" after watching a battle in Baltimore in 1814.

current-affairs.q: In February 2024, which company's Odysseus lander made the first US landing on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972?
current-affairs.fact: Odysseus touched down in the Moon's south polar region but tipped onto its side, yet still sent back data and images.

current-affairs.q: Which historic Maui town, once the royal capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii, was devastated by wildfire in August 2023?
current-affairs.fact: Lahaina's famous banyan tree, planted in 1873, was scorched by the fire but later began sprouting new leaves.

current-affairs.q: On January 6, 2021, rioters breached which building in Washington, D.C., during the certification of the 2020 election results?
current-affairs.fact: Congress resumed its session that night and completed the certification of the Electoral College results early on January 7.

current-affairs.q: Which company launched NASA astronauts to the International Space Station in May 2020, the first crewed orbital launch from US soil since 2011?
current-affairs.fact: Astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley flew in a Crew Dragon capsule they named "Endeavour."

current-affairs.q: Who was sworn in as US Vice President in January 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Before entering politics, the former Ohio senator wrote the bestselling 2016 memoir "Hillbilly Elegy."

current-affairs.q: Which singer's Eras Tour, which ended in December 2024, became the highest-grossing concert tour of all time?
current-affairs.fact: The tour grossed over $2 billion across 149 shows on five continents.

current-affairs.q: Which US city was devastated by the Palisades and Eaton wildfires in January 2025?
current-affairs.fact: The fires destroyed thousands of homes and rank among the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

current-affairs.q: Which law, signed in August 2022, contained the largest federal investment in clean energy and climate in US history?
choices: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
current-affairs.fact: Despite its name, much of the law focused on clean-energy tax credits, alongside measures such as Medicare drug-price negotiation.

current-affairs.q: In June 2022, the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in which case?
choices: Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization
current-affairs.fact: The ruling returned the authority to regulate abortion to the individual states.

current-affairs.q: Which NASA mission deliberately crashed a spacecraft into the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos in September 2022?
current-affairs.fact: The impact shortened Dimorphos's orbit around its parent asteroid by about 32 minutes, the first test of planetary defense.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected Speaker of the House in October 2023, after Kevin McCarthy's removal?
current-affairs.fact: McCarthy was the first Speaker in US history to be removed from the post by a vote of the House.

current-affairs.q: Which NASA rocket launched the uncrewed Artemis I mission around the Moon in November 2022?
current-affairs.fact: Its Orion capsule flew about 432,000 km from Earth, farther than any spacecraft built to carry humans had gone before.

current-affairs.q: Which law signed in August 2022 provided about $52 billion to boost US semiconductor manufacturing and research?
choices: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act
current-affairs.fact: CHIPS stands for "Creating Helpful Incentives to Produce Semiconductors."

current-affairs.q: In June 2023, the Supreme Court ended race-conscious college admissions in cases involving Harvard and which other university?
current-affairs.fact: Both cases were brought by the group Students for Fair Admissions.

current-affairs.q: Which NASA spacecraft returned samples from the asteroid Bennu to Earth in September 2023?
current-affairs.fact: The sample capsule landed in the Utah desert; the spacecraft flew on, renamed OSIRIS-APEX, toward the asteroid Apophis.

current-affairs.q: Which Ohio town was hit by a train derailment and release of hazardous chemicals in February 2023?
current-affairs.fact: The Norfolk Southern freight train was carrying vinyl chloride, which crews vented and burned to prevent an explosion.

current-affairs.q: Which Supreme Court justice retired in June 2022, making way for Ketanji Brown Jackson?
current-affairs.fact: Appointed by Bill Clinton in 1994, Breyer served nearly 28 years; Jackson had once clerked for him.

general.q: What is the capital of the United States?
general.fact: D.C. stands for District of Columbia, a federal district that is not part of any state.

general.q: Which is the largest US state by area?
general.fact: Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas, the second-largest state.

general.q: How many stars are on the current US flag?
general.fact: The 13 stripes stand for the original colonies; the 50-star design adopted in 1960 is the flag's 27th official version.

general.q: In which city's harbor does the Statue of Liberty stand?
general.fact: A gift from France dedicated in 1886, the statue was designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with an inner framework by Gustave Eiffel.

general.q: Which park, established in 1872, is widely considered the world's first national park?
general.fact: Yellowstone sits atop a volcanic hotspot and holds roughly half of the world's geysers, including Old Faithful.

general.q: Which sport did James Naismith invent in 1891?
general.fact: Naismith, a Canadian-born teacher in Springfield, Massachusetts, used peach baskets as the first hoops.

general.q: Which of the Great Lakes lies entirely within the United States?
general.fact: Together, the five Great Lakes hold about a fifth of the world's fresh surface water.

general.q: Which was the most recent state to join the United States, in August 1959?
general.fact: Hawaii is the only US state made up entirely of islands, and Hawaiian is an official state language alongside English.

general.q: What is the highest peak in the contiguous United States (excluding Alaska and Hawaii)?
general.fact: California's Mount Whitney (4,421 m) lies less than 140 km from Badwater Basin in Death Valley, the lowest point in North America.

general.q: What is the official national motto of the United States, adopted in 1956?
general.fact: "E pluribus unum" ("Out of many, one") was the traditional motto and still appears on the Great Seal of the United States.

general.q: Which famous Arizona canyon was carved by the Colorado River?
general.fact: The Grand Canyon is about 446 km (277 miles) long and up to about 1.8 km (6,000 ft) deep.

general.q: Which US holiday falls on the fourth Thursday of November?
general.fact: Lincoln proclaimed a national Thanksgiving in 1863; Congress fixed it to the fourth Thursday of November in 1941.

general.q: Which US city is nicknamed "The Windy City"?
general.fact: Chicago isn't actually the windiest US city; the nickname may have poked fun at its boastful politicians.

general.q: How many presidents' faces are carved into Mount Rushmore?
general.fact: Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln gaze out over South Dakota's Black Hills; each face is about 60 feet (18 m) tall.

general.q: Which city is home to the Golden Gate Bridge?
general.fact: Opened in 1937, the bridge is painted a custom color called "International Orange" to stand out in the fog.

general.q: Which is the most populous US state?
general.fact: More than 39 million people live in California, over one-tenth of all Americans.

general.q: Which California valley holds the lowest point in North America?
general.fact: Badwater Basin lies 86 m (282 ft) below sea level, less than 140 km from Mount Whitney, the highest point in the lower 48.

general.q: In which city is the Kentucky Derby run each year?
general.fact: Raced at Churchill Downs since 1875, the Derby is nicknamed "the most exciting two minutes in sports."

general.q: Which famous highway, established in 1926, ran from Chicago to Santa Monica, California?
general.fact: Bypassed by the Interstates, Route 66 was officially decommissioned in 1985, but its old roadside diners and motels still draw travelers.

general.q: In which state are the Everglades?
general.fact: The Everglades are often described as the only place on Earth where alligators and crocodiles live side by side.

general.q: What is the deepest lake in the United States?
general.fact: Oregon's Crater Lake, 594 m (1,949 ft) deep, fills the caldera left when the volcano Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago.

general.q: Founded in 1565, which is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the contiguous United States?
general.fact: The Florida city was founded by Spanish admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, 42 years before Jamestown.

general.q: Which team won the first modern World Series, in 1903?
general.fact: Boston beat Pittsburgh five games to three in a best-of-nine series; the Americans were later renamed the Red Sox.

general.q: Delicate Arch, a famous freestanding sandstone arch, is in which state?
general.fact: It stands in Arches National Park, which holds more than 2,000 documented natural stone arches.

general.q: The Appalachian Trail runs from Georgia to which state?
general.fact: The roughly 3,500 km (2,200-mile) footpath ends at the summit of Mount Katahdin.
